# Abstract

Southern India below the Krishna-Tungabhadra frontier constitutes one of the most resilient agrarian and commercial environments in early modern Asia. Encompassing 167.458 km² across 1.989 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells, the territory spanning modern Tamil Nadu and Kerala combines two sharply differentiated ecological systems: the narrow, hyper-humid coastal strip of Malabar and Travancore backed by the rainforest-clad ramparts of the Western Ghats, and the broader, sub-humid to semi-arid plains of the Coromandel coast, drained by the seasonal Kaveri, Palar, Ponnaiyar and Vaigai river basins. Across the three centuries separating the peak of Vijayanagara suzerainty in 1526AD from the definitive British annexation of the Carnatic in 1801AD, regional population expanded from 12,8M to 20,5M inhabitants, raising aggregate settlement density from 76,44 to 122,42 persons per km². This demographic increase of 60,16% proceeded at a long-term compound rate of 0,17% per annum, reflecting sustained agrarian frontier expansion, the proliferation of communal irrigation cascades and intense commercial integration with Indian Ocean mercantile networks.

Demographic mass remained concentrated in the fertile alluvial basins and coastal trading corridors. The Carnatic Nawabdom, Gingee, Tanjore and Coromandel province accommodated 5,63M people in 1526AD (44% of regional population; 66,31 persons per km²), expanding to 6,38M in 1600AD, 6,95M in 1650AD, 7,57M in 1700AD, 8,18M in 1750AD and 9,02M by 1801AD (106,2 persons per km²). This eastern zone was anchored by the colonial port of Chennai, whose rapid rise following its 1639AD foundation brought its urban populace to 325,77k in 1700AD before late eighteenth-century wartime disruptions lowered it to 251,87k in 1801AD, alongside established inland craft and religious centres including Tiruchirappalli (73,82k in 1801AD) and Kanchipuram (60k). The southwestern maritime corridor of Travancore, Cochin and Zamorin Malabar supported 3,71M inhabitants in 1526AD (29%; 101,31 persons per km²), rising steadily to 4,21M in 1600AD, 4,58M in 1650AD, 4,99M in 1700AD, 5,39M in 1750AD and 5,95M in 1801AD (162,25 persons per km²), sustaining the highest rural densities in peninsular India through intensive garden cultivation and pepper commerce centred on Kozhikode (48,3k) and Thiruvananthapuram. The southern interior territory of the Madurai Nayaka kingdom and Tirunelveli supported 3,46M people in 1526AD (27%; 75,32 persons per km²), rising to 3,92M in 1600AD, 4,27M in 1650AD, 4,64M in 1700AD, 5,02M in 1750AD and 5,54M in 1801AD (120,62 persons per km²), anchored by the deltaic capital of Thanjavur (77,28k in 1650AD, 52,31k in 1801AD) and the temple metropolis of Madurai (75k).

This demographic synthesis combines 335 catalogued settlements with temple epigraphy, Jesuit mission letters, Dutch East India Company archival rolls, Arcot Nawabdom fiscal accounts and early British collectorate surveys under INDUS. By subtracting georeferenced urban centres from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the model separates urbanisation pulses from underlying agricultural expansion. The trajectory demonstrates that despite severe mid-eighteenth-century military shocks and recurring monsoonal droughts, the southern agrarian base preserved long-term continuity through collective water governance, flexible dryland cropping and regional trade circuits.

# Background

## Agro-Ecological Divergence across the Western Ghats

The physical geography of southern India is structured by the orographic barrier of the Western Ghats, which divide the subcontinent into two distinct environmental regimes [@Casile2021Climatic; @Kramrisch1953Dravida]. On the windward western coast, Kerala receives between 2.000 mm and 3.500 mm of precipitation annually during the southwest monsoon (June to September). This torrential rainfall feeds short, rapid perennial rivers including the Periyar, Bharathappuzha and Pamba, creating a narrow littoral of coastal lagoons, backwaters (*kayals*) and fertile lateritic foothills. Agriculture in this western belt was organised around permanent tree crops (coconut, areca nut, jackfruit), intensive spice cultivation (black pepper, cardamom, ginger) and terraced wet-paddy farming [@M2026Politics; @Jacob2025Protesta]. The lack of nucleated villages in Kerala, where dispersed homesteads (*parambus*) stretched continuously along waterways, reflected an ecological setting where irrigation tanks were unnecessary and settlement followed linear garden tracts.

East of the Ghats, the Tamil country occupies a vast rain-shadow plain that receives minimal moisture from the southwest monsoon, depending instead on cyclonic storms delivered by the retreating northeast monsoon between October and December. Annual rainfall declines to between 600 mm and 1.000 mm across the interior tablelands of Coimbatore, Madurai and Tirunelveli, dropping below 600 mm in rain-shadow pockets. Consequently, agriculture in Tamil Nadu was divided into two distinct ecological zones: wet tracts (*nanjai*) irrigated by perennial river diversions and extensive tank cascades, and dry uplands (*punjai*) dependent on erratic seasonal rainfall and deep well irrigation [@Stein1966Land; @Lakshminarayan2018Great]. This environmental dichotomy shaped distinct demographic densities, social structures and land-tenure relations between the fertile alluvial river corridors and the surrounding dry scrub plains.

## The Kaveri Delta, Tank Cascades and Palar Basin

The agricultural heartland of southern India was anchored by the Kaveri River, whose delta formed the granary of the Tamil country [@Thilagavathy2026Evolutio]. Originating in the Kodagu highlands of Karnataka, the Kaveri enters the Tamil plains through the Hogenakkal gorge and divides near Tiruchirappalli into two principal branches: the northern Coleroon (*Kollidam*), which functions primarily as a flood escape, and the southern Kaveri proper, which bifurcates into hundreds of distributary channels across the Thanjavur alluvial plain. Hydraulic management of this delta relied on ancient weir installations, most notably the Grand Anicut (*Kallanai*), supplemented by an elaborate network of diversion channels, sluices (*madagus*) and drainage canals that permitted continuous double-cropping of wet rice (*samba* and *kuruvai*).

Beyond the perennial reach of the Kaveri, agrarian communities across the Palar, Ponnaiyar and Vaigai basins engineered massive cascades of interconnected earthen reservoirs (*eris*). In these systems, surplus runoff from upper tanks fed lower reservoirs through contour channels, recharging the local water table and securing irrigation for winter paddy crops [@Thilagavathy2026Evolutio; @Frykenberg1967Studies]. In the semi-arid dry tracts, cultivators relied on drought-resistant millets, including sorghum (*cholam*), finger millet (*ragi*) and pearl millet (*cumbu*), supplemented by sesame, pulses and cotton. Communal maintenance of irrigation works, coordinated by village assemblies (*urs* and *sabhas*) and temple corporations, formed the institutional foundation of agrarian demographic stability across centuries of dynastic transformation.

## Textile Artisanal Networks and Proto-Industrial Weaving Centres

In addition to food-grain cultivation, early modern southern India supported an extensive rural textile industry that underpinned commercial urbanization [@Bulten2025Book; @Bagchi1978Needed]. In the dry red and black soils (*regur*) of the interior tablelands, particularly around Coimbatore, Salem, Tirunelveli and the Palar Valley, peasant households cultivated commercial cotton alongside food grains. Cotton cultivation provided raw material for specialised weaving castes, predominantly the *kaikkolars*, *saliyars* and *devangas*, who operated thousands of handlooms in market villages and urban textile wards (*pettais*) [@Stein1966Land; @KK2025Colonial].

These artisanal networks were intimately integrated into agricultural life. Weaving communities maintained close ties with cotton cultivators and dyers (*chayakarars*), utilising local vegetable dyes such as chay-root (*Oldenlandia umbellata*) and indigo. Market towns such as Salem, Karur, Kanchipuram and Madurai operated as textile aggregation centres, where merchant guilds (*chettis* and *komatis*) advanced raw cotton and grain to weavers against guaranteed deliveries of finished piece-goods. The resulting fabrics, including painted calicoes, chintz and fine muslins, formed the principal currency of exchange with European chartered trading companies and Southeast Asian maritime traders, sustaining liquid cash inflows that supported monetization and agrarian tax payments across the region [@Bulten2025Book; @Bagchi1978Needed].

## Political Fragmentation and Nayaka State Formation

The political landscape of southern India was transformed by the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire following the decisive defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565AD [@Frykenberg1967Studies; @Bagchi1978Needed]. During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, Vijayanagara emperors had established military governors (*nayakas*) across the Tamil country to garrison border fortresses and supervise tax collection. With the dissolution of central imperial authority, these regional governors transformed their administrative commands into autonomous hereditary dynasties, establishing powerful kingdoms centered at Gingee (Senji), Thanjavur and Madurai.

The Nayaka era was characterised by vigorous agrarian colonisation of inland scrub forests and dry upland frontiers. Telugu-speaking warrior-cultivators (*kavalkars*, *kammavars* and *reddis*) migrated southwards along the central plateau, clearing scrub forests, excavating large masonry irrigation wells and establishing fortified agrarian villages (*palayams*) governed by local chieftains (*poligars*) [@Frykenberg1967Studies; @Stein1966Land]. The Madurai Nayakas, particularly during the reign of Tirumala Nayaka (1623AD to 1659AD), constructed monumental fortresses, palace complexes and grand temple pavilions (*mandapams*), investing royal capital into temple trusts that redistributed agrarian resources and sponsored commercial settlements (*pettais*) throughout the southern dry zone.

## Maritime Littorals, Factory Enclaves and Colonial Penetration

Along the coasts, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries brought increasing interaction with European chartered trading companies [@Bulten2025Book; @KK2025Colonial]. On the Malabar coast, Portuguese attempts to monopolise the spice trade provoked prolonged naval conflicts with the Zamorins of Calicut, culminating in the rise of alternative emporia at Cochin, Cannanore and Kollam. By the mid-seventeenth century, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) displaced the Portuguese from Cochin (1663AD) and established trading factories along the Coromandel coast at Pulicat, Sadras and Nagapattinam, while the Danish East India Company occupied Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) in 1620AD and the French established Pondicherry (Puducherry) in 1674AD.

The English East India Company secured a land grant at Madraspatnam in 1639AD, constructing Fort St. George and founding the settlement of Madras (Chennai). The British enclave attracted thousands of indigenous weavers (*kaikkolars*), merchants (*chettis*) and dyers, transforming a collection of fishing hamlets into an expansive textile export hub producing painted calicoes and fine muslins for overseas markets [@Bulten2025Book; @Bagchi1978Needed]. During the eighteenth century, the disintegration of the Mughal Empire after the death of Aurangzeb brought the Carnatic under the autonomous rule of the Nawabs of Arcot. Subsequent Anglo-French imperial rivalry erupted in the Carnatic Wars (1746AD to 1763AD), which devastated rural districts and entangled regional rulers in crippling military debts, culminating in the formal annexation of the Carnatic by the British East India Company in 1801AD [@Bulten2025Book; @Frykenberg1967Studies].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To reconstruct demographic densities across 167.458 km² of terrestrial surface, the INDUS spatial engine partitions the southern Indian subcontinent into 1.989 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to perennial rivers (the Kaveri, Vaigai, Tambraparni, Periyar and Bharathappuzha) and seasonal stream networks, with density attenuation calibrated against historical canal distribution records [@Thilagavathy2026Evolutio].
- Floodplain and delta geomasking: continuous weighting identifying active alluvium, silt-renewed river terraces and coastal deltaic flats capable of sustaining intensive double-cropping.
- Topographic slope: penalising the steep, forested slopes of the Western Ghats (Anamalai, Nilgiri, Palani and Cardamom hills) while favouring flat alluvial plains, coastal strips and gently undulating tablelands.
- Bioclimatic suitability: incorporating seasonal precipitation models that account for both southwest and northeast monsoon regimes across the trans-Ghat environmental gradient [@Casile2021Climatic].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 335 catalogued settlements with longitudinal population series are anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements within each sub-region is aggregated and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing step discontinuities along administrative boundaries and mountain ranges.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 14% across all benchmark years from 1526AD to 1801AD). At the 1526AD baseline, the regional total of 12,8M is bounded between 11,01M and 14,59M inhabitants; at the 1801AD terminus, the total of 20,5M is bounded between 17,63M and 23,37M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates historical variances across temple donor records, tax registers, household multiplier assumptions and early colonial collectorate censuses [@Stein1966Land; @Harnetty1993Land].

# Testing and Validation

## Archival and Epigraphic Ground-Truthing

Reconstructing demographic trajectories across early modern South Asia requires reconciliation of diverse archival traditions [@Journal2025; @TAHIR2021Translatio]. In Tamil Nadu, thousands of stone and copper-plate inscriptions (*shasanas*) preserved on temple walls record land grants, tax exemptions, canal excavations and occupational distributions among weaving communities, artisans and agricultural labourers [@Journal2025; @Stein1966Land]. These epigraphic records demonstrate steady settlement expansion throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, particularly in the dry tablelands where Nayaka chieftains established new commercial settlements (*pettais*) and granted hereditary rights to warrior-colonists.

For the western coast, palm-leaf records (*cadjan* or *grandhas*) preserved in temple archives and state repositories provide detailed accounts of pepper yields, garden property transfers and maritime customs revenues [@M2026Politics]. These indigenous sources are corroborated by foreign mercantile documentation. The Dutch East India Company maintained regular censuses of domestic hearths and slave populations in Cochin and surrounding coastal districts, while the letters of Jesuit missionaries in the Madurai Mission (founded in 1606AD by Roberto de Nobili) describe urban life, royal succession crises and agrarian distress during severe drought years [@Jacob2025Protesta; @Kramrisch1954Dravida].

## Agrarian Yields and Caloric Carrying Capacity

The plausibility of demographic growth from 12,8M to 20,5M inhabitants was tested against caloric carrying capacity models based on historical crop yields and cattle energy inputs [@T1945Crossbre; @Lakshminarayan2018Great]. In the Kaveri delta, double-cropped wet paddy under canal irrigation yielded between 1,8 and 2,4 tonnes of unhusked grain (*paddy*) per hectare, sufficient to support rural population densities exceeding 250 persons per km² on prime alluvium [@Stein1966Land; @Thilagavathy2026Evolutio]. In the dry upland tracts, mixed cropping of sorghum, finger millet and pulses produced between 0,6 and 0,9 tonnes per hectare, supporting lower densities between 70 and 110 persons per km².

Draught cattle played a critical role in South Indian agricultural ecology [@T1945Crossbre]. The hardy Kangayam and Amrit Mahal breeds were reared in the dry upland pastures of Coimbatore and the Mysore plateau before being traded into the Kaveri delta for heavy ploughing in muddy paddy soils. The integration of livestock husbandry with tank agriculture ensured nitrogen replenishment through manure application, maintaining soil fertility across centuries of intensive cultivation [@T1945Crossbre; @Stein1966Land].

## Mortality Shocks, Famines and Epidemic Distortions

Demographic expansion was punctuated by recurring subsistence crises and wartime mortalities [@Casile2021Climatic; @Vincent1947French]. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries witnessed several severe famine episodes caused by failure of the northeast monsoon:
- The famine of 1630AD to 1631AD, which affected western India and extended into the northern Carnatic, disrupting handloom weaving and commercial agriculture [@Bulten2025Book].
- The prolonged drought of 1686AD to 1688AD during Aurangzeb's siege of Golconda and subsequent southern campaigns, which caused catastrophic grain shortages across the Coromandel coast [@Frykenberg1967Studies].
- The great drought of 1709AD to 1711AD, documented in Jesuit mission records as having depopulated rural districts in Madurai and Thanjavur [@Jacob2025Protesta].
- The devastating Carnatic famine of 1782AD to 1783AD, precipitated by the scorched-earth tactics of Hyder Ali's cavalry during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, which displaced over 200k rural cultivators and caused widespread mortality in Madras and Arcot [@Bagchi1978Needed; @Bulten2025Book].

Mortality was amplified by epidemic disease, notably smallpox, cholera and endemic malarial fevers in riverine deltas and forest margins [@DV2025Physicia; @Siena2024Moral]. In response, indigenous medical practitioners (*siddha* and *ayurvedic* vaidyas) developed pharmacopoeias utilising regional herbal preparations and mineral compounds to combat epidemic outbreaks [@DV2025Physicia]. Despite these severe periodic setbacks, demographic growth resumed rapidly during favourable monsoon years, supported by high marital fertility, customary adoption practices and rural labour mobility [@Vincent1947French; @Baugh1978Decelera].

## Asymptotic Saturation of the Source Ledger

The INDUS source ledger was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to ensure comprehensive geographic coverage:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census tables (Census of India Table A04 Class I to VI, 1901 to 2011), establishing historical continuity for 208 primary urban localities.
- Wave 2: Extraction of settlement catalogues from archival monographs, epigraphic surveys and institutional gazetteers, adding 90 pre-modern towns.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, incorporating 37 early Nayaka fortress towns, coastal ports and market villages.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps across all three divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 611 candidate localities were audited: 335 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 276 were excluded (predominantly duplicate administrative aliases within a 2,2 km spatial radius and non-habitation localities).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of southern India from 1526AD to 1801AD demonstrates continuous expansion across all three sub-regions (Figure \ref{fig:demography} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}). Over the 275-year period, regional population expanded from 12,8M to 20,5M, with density increasing from 76,44 to 122,42 persons per km².

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### The Late Vijayanagara and Early Nayaka Consolidation (1526AD to 1600AD)

Between 1526AD and 1600AD, regional population expanded from 12,8M to 14,5M (yielding an aggregate density of 86,59 persons per km²). This initial epoch was defined by the institutional consolidation of the southern Nayaka realms following the defeat of Vijayanagara central authority in 1565AD [@Frykenberg1967Studies]. The Nayakas of Gingee, Thanjavur and Madurai acted as patron-monarchs, clearing peripheral scrub forests, establishing new settlement colonies and extending irrigation works. In Thanjavur, Nayaka rulers repaired Kaveri canals and invited Telugu agriculturalists to settle the delta, causing urban population to expand from 52,31k to 67,21k. In Madurai, Tirumala Nayaka's predecessors laid out expansive temple precincts and market streets, raising the city population from 58,5k to 75k. On the western coast, Kozhikode flourished under the Zamorins, its population growing from 32,69k to 42,01k through sustained trade with Arab, Persian and Gujarati merchants [@M2026Politics].

### The Seventeenth-Century Commercial and Agrarian Climax (1600AD to 1700AD)

Between 1600AD and 1700AD, population expanded from 14,5M to 17,2M (102,71 persons per km²). This century witnessed the maturation of coastal commercial networks and the rise of European factory enclaves [@Bulten2025Book; @KK2025Colonial]. The foundation of Madras (Chennai) by the English in 1639AD stimulated massive inward migration of artisans and merchants; by 1650AD, the settlement accommodated 265,19k people, climbing to a pre-modern peak of 325,77k by 1700AD. Handloom textile production boomed across the Coromandel hinterland, where weaving hamlets specialised in indigo dyeing and fine cloth manufacture for global trade [@Bulten2025Book; @Bagchi1978Needed]. In the Kaveri delta, Thanjavur reached its all-time demographic peak of 77,28k in 1650AD under late Nayaka rule before Maratha conquest in 1674AD established a new royal administration. Despite monsoonal variations and Mughal incursions under Aurangzeb in the 1680s and 1690s, the regional agrarian base supported steady demographic expansion [@Frykenberg1967Studies].

### Eighteenth-Century Poligar Conflicts and Travancore Consolidation (1700AD to 1750AD)

Between 1700AD and 1750AD, regional population increased from 17,2M to 18,6M (111,07 persons per km²). Growth proceeded at a slightly decelerated pace due to political instability in the Carnatic and recurring military conflicts among regional chieftains [@Bagchi1978Needed; @Baugh1978Decelera]. Following the disintegration of central Mughal control, the Nawabs of Arcot established an autonomous dynasty, competing with local *poligars* for tax revenues across the Palar and Ponnaiyar basins.

In dramatic contrast to the fragmented Carnatic, southwestern India experienced political centralisation under Marthanda Varma of Travancore (1729AD to 1758AD) [@M2026Politics; @Jacob2025Protesta]. Defeating feudal barons (*Ettuveetil Pillamar*) and shattering Dutch naval dominance at the historic Battle of Colachel in 1741AD, Marthanda Varma created a centralised state administration. He established state monopolies over pepper, tobacco and timber, constructed granaries and royal supply depots, and dedicated the kingdom to Lord Padmanabha in 1750AD [@M2026Politics; @Kramrisch1953Dravida]. These administrative reforms insulated Travancore from exterior predation, raising its sub-regional population from 4,99M to 5,39M between 1700AD and 1750AD.

### The Anglo-Mysore Wars and Colonial Revenue Settlement (1750AD to 1801AD)

Between 1750AD and 1801AD, population expanded from 18,6M to 20,5M (122,42 persons per km²). This concluding epoch was marked by violent imperial contests: the Carnatic Wars between Britain and France, the incursions of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore into Malabar and the Tamil plains, and the Poligar Wars in Tirunelveli and Ramanathapuram [@Frykenberg1967Studies; @Saravanan2006Colonial]. Military campaigns inflicted severe localized destruction; Chennai's population contracted from 313,65k in 1750AD to 251,87k in 1801AD following sieges, blockades and rural flight, while Thanjavur receded from 62,58k to 52,31k.

However, the military subjugation of the southern *poligars* by British forces under Colonel Fullarton and Arthur Wellesley, followed by the formal annexation of the Carnatic in 1801AD, inaugurated a new administrative era [@Frykenberg1967Studies; @Crane1966Land]. The British East India Company established the Madras Presidency, replacing indirect tribute extraction with direct collectorate governance. Under Thomas Munro, the administration introduced the *ryotwari* settlement system, surveying field boundaries, registering individual landholders (*ryots*) and fixing monetary tax assessments [@Frykenberg1967Studies; @Stein1966Land; @Crane1966Landb]. By 1801AD, demographic mass in the Carnatic reached 9,02M, while Travancore and Malabar reached 5,95M, laying the administrative and spatial framework for nineteenth-century colonial censuses [@Harnetty1993Land; @Saravanan2006Colonial].

The settlement hierarchy displays two distinct urban traditions:
1. Ancient sacred and royal capitals located on perennial river systems, such as Thanjavur, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli and Kanchipuram. These centres combined monumental temple architecture with extensive market quarters, housing populations between 50k and 75k people throughout the early modern era.
2. Colonial and indigenous maritime port cities, such as Chennai, Kozhikode, Kochi and Puducherry. Chennai achieved pre-eminence through its export textile manufacturing and political role as the headquarters of the British East India Company, reaching over 300k inhabitants at its eighteenth-century peak.

Secondary market towns (*pettais*) and fortified garrison nodes formed an extensive middle tier in the regional urban network [@Stein1966Land; @Bulten2025Book]. Towns such as Salem, Karur, Dindigul, Kumbakonam, Nagapattinam, Cuddalore and Arcot accommodated between 15k and 40k inhabitants, functioning as regional collection centres where agricultural surpluses, raw cotton, handloom textiles and spices were exchanged. Periodic rural markets (*shandies*), held on rotating days across adjacent villages, linked isolated farming homesteads to this secondary urban network, facilitating commodity circulation and tax monetization across peninsular South Asia [@Stein1966Land; @Frykenberg1967Studies].

# Limitations

Several methodological constraints qualify this historical demographic reconstruction:
- Epigraphic survival bias: stone and copper-plate inscriptions are disproportionately clustered around wealthy temple establishments in wet-paddy river basins, leaving semi-arid upland dry tracts and pastoral frontiers under-represented in pre-eighteenth-century epigraphic sources [@Journal2025; @Stein1966Land].
- Gaps in indigenous cadastral records: palm-leaf village accounts (*karanams*) have suffered heavy decay from tropical humidity and insect damage, forcing demographic reconstructions to rely on secondary summaries compiled during early British revenue surveys [@Frykenberg1967Studies].
- Fluctuating urban boundaries: pre-modern Indian cities lacked formal municipal limits; calculating urban populations requires assumptions regarding household multipliers (typically 4,8 to 5,5 persons per hearth) and distinguishing permanent urban residents from seasonal pilgrimage crowds and floating artisan populations [@Thompson1991Sallusti; @Bulten2025Book].
- Trans-maritime migration: maritime migration across the Palk Strait between Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka (Jaffna), as well as labour mobility along the Malabar littoral, introduces unrecorded population movements during acute drought years [@Kurinjivendan2022Indian].
- Price fluctuations and silver inflows: monetary inflation driven by foreign silver imports through European factory trade altered real wages and rural tax burdens, potentially influencing household formation rates across commercial weaving districts [@Bagchi1978Needed; @KK2025Colonial].
- Pastoralist invisibility: mobile pastoral communities, such as the Kurumbas and Idaiyans who grazed sheep and cattle across the semi-arid dry tracts, moved seasonally and were systematically excluded from village cadastral accounts [@T1945Crossbre; @Stein1966Land].

# Conclusion

The demographic trajectory of Tamil Nadu and Kerala between 1526AD and 1801AD illustrates the enduring resilience of southern South Asian agrarian systems. Supported by communal tank cascades in the Tamil dry tracts, perennial river diversions in the Kaveri delta and intensive spice-garden agroforestry along the Malabar littoral, regional population expanded from 12,8M to 20,5M inhabitants over 275 years. This growth proceeded despite profound political reorganisation following the disintegration of the Vijayanagara Empire, the rise and fall of autonomous Nayaka kingdoms, and the destructive military campaigns of the eighteenth century. By anchoring 335 catalogued settlements to their geographic coordinates and dasymetrically allocating residual rural cultivators, the INDUS reconstruction establishes a quantitative spatial foundation for understanding pre-colonial South Indian demography.

# Appendix

## Regional Parameters and Bounding Coordinates

The spatial reconstruction is anchored by three sub-regional entities within the INDUS GIS framework:
- Travancore, Cochin and Malabar (entity tam3_travancore_malabar): 36.640 km², 439 cells. Bounding box: latitude 8,33° N to 12,75° N, longitude 74,92° E to 77,42° E.
- Carnatic, Gingee, Tanjore and Coromandel (entity tam3_carnatic_tanjore): 84.932 km², 1.007 cells. Bounding box: latitude 10,17° N to 16,75° N, longitude 75,25° E to 82,25° E.
- Madurai Nayaka and Tirunelveli (entity tam3_madurai_nayaka): 45.886 km², 543 cells. Bounding box: latitude 8,08° N to 11,33° N, longitude 76,83° E to 79,83° E.

Aggregate land area equals 167.458 km², encompassing 1.989 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells.

## Sub-Regional Allocation Principles

Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against dasymetric suitability weights reflecting elevation, slope, hydrographic proximity and soil productivity. Settlements with known coordinates are directly subtracted from sub-regional totals prior to continuous surface interpolation, ensuring full accounting between nucleated urban inhabitants and rural cultivators across all benchmark horizons.

## Cartographic Datums and Spatial Calibration

Spatial geometries and coastline definitions follow the INDUS GIS repository, projected under the Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area projection centered on 11° N, 78° E. Regional boundaries align with historical eighteenth-century administrative divisions recorded in the Survey of India historical map archives and East India Company collectorate records.
